title: Cordless phone: NiMH cells, speaker, microphone, screen and adapters
summary: A cordless home phone is a base and one or more handsets, each with a pair of NiMH AAA cells, a speaker, a microphone, a small LCD and a radio that only talks to its own base, plus plug-in adapters and charging cradles. Five to ten minutes with a small screwdriver. The dangers are small: leaking cells and the old heavy plug-in adapters.

steps.text: Test it before you strip it. Plug the base in and put the handset on its cradle. If it switches on and links to the base, keep the set whole: base and handset make a short-range voice link, and handsets of some models can call each other (intercom) with no phone line. See notes.
Unplug the adapter from the wall, and unplug the phone line from the wall jack and from the base, before you open anything. Take the handset off the cradle.
steps.warn: A live phone line carries about 50 V DC and rings at around 90 V AC: enough for a nasty shock. Unplug it at the wall jack, not only at the base.

steps.text: Open the battery door on the handset and take out the cells. Most handsets hold 2 AAA NiMH cells (2.4 V). Older ones use NiCd cells (labelled NiCd or Ni-Cd) or a flat pack on a plug.
steps.warn: Leaking cells leave white or green crust that burns skin and eyes. Wear gloves, keep hands off your face and wash up afterwards.

steps.text: Test each cell: a good NiMH cell reads 1.2–1.4 V. A cell near zero volts may recover on a slow charge; a cell that is hot, swollen or leaking is finished. Read the capacity (mAh) on the label. Keep NiCd cells whole: they hold cadmium.
Open the handset. Take out the screws, usually under the battery door and in the belt-clip slot. Then work a flat blade or plastic tool along the seam from the bottom to release the clips.

Lift out the board. The earpiece speaker is held by a bracket or foam, with 2 wires or contacts. The microphone is a small round capsule in a rubber boot near the bottom: pop it out and keep the boot. Cut wires leaving about 5 cm.
The LCD is a small glass screen held by clips, often on rubber contact strips. Lift it out gently by its frame and keep the strips with it. Don't touch the glass.
Keep each handset's board, and the base's board, whole and together. The radio and antenna are a matched pair with the base and can't be reused with other radios.

Base: take out the screws underneath and lift the board out. Older bases carry a small speaker, a ringer and a tape or memory chip for the answering machine. Keep the board with the radio and antenna attached.

Plug-in adapters and charging cradles: read each label (volts, amps, and AC or DC output) and write it on with a marker. Older adapters are heavy iron transformers with an AC output. Newer ones are small DC switch-mode supplies. Keep cradles whole: each is a small trickle charger for 2 NiMH AAA cells.
steps.warn: Don't open wall adapters. They carry mains inside even when they look harmless.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **NiMH cells.** AAA rechargeables, 1.2 V each, usually 400–800 mAh. Good ones go in flashlights and radios. Charge them only with a NiMH charger, never a lithium one.
- **A working set.** Base and handset make a private cable-free voice link across a house or yard, about 50–300 m depending on walls. A second handset gives you a handset-to-handset intercom on models that allow it. Keep the adapter that powers the base.
- **Speaker and microphone.** A small speaker and an electret microphone make a tiny intercom, a listening post or an alarm. The microphone needs 2–5 V through a resistor to work.
- **LCD.** A small display for a project, but only with the board it came with. Keep them together.
- **Adapters.** Typically 5–9 V at a few hundred milliamps. Check the label: an AC adapter will damage anything that needs DC.
- **Cradles.** A charger for 2 NiMH AAA cells at about 100–200 mA.

## Variations

- US phones are usually DECT 6.0 (1.9 GHz). European DECT uses 1.88 GHz. Older sets use 900 MHz, 2.4 GHz or 5.8 GHz.
- Phones with an answering machine have a small tape or flash memory chip in the base. Neither is worth much.
- Some handsets hold a flat battery pack (3.6 V NiMH) instead of two AAA cells. Treat it as a NiMH cell pack.

## What to leave

- The rubber keypad and plastic shells.
- Leaking cells with heavy crust.
